newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italian metalworkers call strike over pay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italian metalworkers call strike over pay.

text.p: Italian trades unions representing 1.5 million engineering and metalworkers on Monday called an eight-hour strike on September 27 in support of a pay claim.

It will be the sector's first nationwide strike over contracts since November 1990 and a blow to Italy's centre-left government, which wants unions to accept moderate wage increases to help the fight against inflation.
Metalworkers at key Italian industrial companies such as carmaker Fiat and information technology group Olivetti have demanded an overall wage rise of 10.1 percent over the next two years.
Employers' group Federmeccanica has offered increases of between seven and nine percent -- in line with contracts already renewed in various other Italian sectors.
Talks between unions and Federmeccanica, suspended in July, are due to resume on Thursday, but the major FIOM, FIM and UILM unions decided to call the strike ahead of the new round.

"From initial informal contacts with Federmeccanica and also from their public declarations it is absolutely clear that the differences which prevented a deal in July remain exactly the same," said Luigi Angeletti, leader of the UILM.
"These are irreconcilable positions and that is why we have called the strike," he told a news conference.

At the heart of the dispute lies a union demand that their members should be compensated in full for a 4.1 percent loss of purchasing power during the old contract period of June 1994-June 1996, when inflation was higher than expected.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government, which has pinned much of its economic programme on slashing inflation, hopes that the metalworkers will follow the example of other sectors and accept slightly lower compensation.

The Treasury wants lower inflation to allow an easing in the interest rates that Italy has to pay on his huge budget deficit. Inflation in August fell to 3.4 percent year-on-year after 3.6 percent in July.
Metalworker unions argue that a 1993 law, which scrapped index-linked pay rises but ruled that higher-than-forecast inflation should be covered in full, must be honoured.
The long-threatened strike will come at a bad time for industry, which is struggling in the face of sluggish economic growth.
Italian gross domestic product (GDP) fell 0.5 percent in the second quarter of 1996 against the first three months and a further decline is expected this quarter.

Industrialists argue that the economic downturn prevents a more generous pay claim and say rising labour costs, coupled with recent rises in the value of the lira will wipe out past competitive gains.

Italian unions last called mass strikes in 1994 to protest at plans by the conservative government of Silvio Berlusconi to overhaul the state pensions system. The plans were eventually redrawn following lengthy negotiations with the unions.

Prodi's government, which includes the former communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), has sought to avoid head-on conflict with the unions. It is involved in lengthy round-table talks with them aimed at boosting employment.
